headline: Fort Trumbull's Cool Seam Keeps Bass Honest While the Sound Cooks
subhead: A three-degree edge at the river mouth and a full-moon current are buying daytime bites the open Sound can't offer right now.
body_markdown:
I stood on the seawall at Fort Trumbull Tuesday morning watching the ebb pile against the point, and you could see the line where it happens — the darker, cooler water sliding out of the river meeting the flatter green stuff off the Ledge Light channel. That seam has been the difference-maker all week. New London's reading right around 70 degrees at the mouth, while Kings Point over on the west end of the Sound is pushing 72 and a half. Three degrees doesn't sound like much until you're the fish deciding whether to sit in the sun all day or duck into the river mouth where the current keeps things moving and the temperature stays civil. Right now the bass are voting with their tails, and they're voting for the Thames.

This time of year the open Sound goes quiet during daylight — the bass shut down and wait for low light, same as they do from Jersey up through the Cape. But river mouths and current-swept structure are the exception, and Fort Trumbull is about as good an exception as this coast has to offer. I've been working the rip on the back half of the ebb, anchoring up-current of the point and letting a 1-ounce bucktail with a white curl-tail trailer swing through the seam on a slow lift-and-drop. Twelve to eighteen feet of water, current still hauling, and the fish are stacked right where the flow bends around the old fort wall. Nothing giant — mostly 24 to 30 inches — but a steady pick through the tide change, which is more than I can say for guys who tried the open harbor at noon and came back with nothing to show for it.

Gold Star Bridge has been holding up its end too. The pilings on the downriver side, especially the third and fourth from the Groton shore, are throwing enough current shadow that bass are tucking in tight and ambushing whatever peanut bunker gets swept through. I watched a guide boat working white paddletails on light jigheads — quarter-ounce, maybe three-eighths — right up against the concrete on the last two hours of the ebb, and they were getting bit often enough to keep at it for a solid hour before it went quiet on the slack. Timing matters here more than almost anywhere on the river. Miss the tide window at the bridge and you're just casting at empty concrete.

The full moon has sharpened everything this week — more water moving, harder current, tighter bite windows, but better ones. Dawn and dusk are still your best bets for the river mouth stripers, same pattern holding from here to Montauk. If you can only fish one tide, make it the last two hours of a night or early-morning ebb when the bunker and peanut bunker are getting flushed out past Fort Trumbull and the fish know it.

We flagged this a week back — said the peanut bunker spread would push cocktail blues into the back bays inside two weeks, and it's already showing. The coves off City Pier and up into the mouth of the harbor near the Thames Street docks are thick with snapper blues right now, and there's a noticeable uptick in bigger cocktail-class fish mixed in, 14 to 16 inches, chasing the same bait pods the snappers are working. Small gold Kastmasters and quarter-ounce poppers worked fast on the surface are money for both sizes. Kids on the dock with bobbers and spearing are cleaning up too — it's about as easy an action as this harbor offers all year, and it's a good one to bring a kid out for.

Porgies have settled onto the sandy patches inside the harbor and off Pleasure Beach, six to twelve feet of water, high-low rigs with sandworm or clam. Nothing spectacular in size but steady enough that if the wind's up and you don't want to fight the open Sound, it's a solid fallback. Blackfish are starting to show interest around the riprap at the bridge abutments and the deeper rock piles off Ocean Beach, though it's still early for that pattern to really turn on — I'd call it a bonus fish right now, not a target.

Ocean Beach itself has been quieter than the river — the surf's been mostly schoolies at first light on white soft-plastic swimbaits, nothing to write home about, and the exposed shoreline just isn't holding bait the way the river mouth structure is. If I had one morning this week, I'd spend it at Fort Trumbull on the back of the ebb, and I'd have the bridge pilings as my backup once the current started to lay down.

Looking ahead, the moon's still going to push hard current through the weekend before it starts easing off by midweek. That means the bite windows stay tight and predictable — work the tide changes at the river mouth and the bridge, don't waste tide fishing the middle of the day in open water, and keep an eye on the bunker schools working up past the sub base. If they hold in the river the way they have been, the blues and the bass ought to keep this pattern going through the week. If that bait pushes out toward the Race, I'd expect the action to thin out here and pick up out toward Fishers Island Sound instead.
